tip_title: There Are Add-Ons to Your Home Policy Most People Never Think to Ask About
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: There Are Add-Ons to Your Home Policy Most People Never Think to Ask About**

A standard homeowners policy covers a lot — but it has gaps that endorsements (basically, optional coverage add-ons) can fill. Depending on where you live and what you own, that could mean sewer backup coverage, identity theft protection, equipment breakdown coverage for appliances, or extended replacement cost for personal belongings. These aren't obscure products; most carriers offer them, most people just never get asked. And individually, many of them add a pretty small amount to your annual premium.

If you haven't looked at what add-ons are available on your current policy, that's a ten-minute conversation worth having with your Peachy agent.

📖 [Learn more from Consumer Reports](https://www.consumerreports.org/money/homeowners-insurance/buying-guide/)
summary: Covers homeowners insurance endorsements (sewer backup, identity theft, equipment breakdown, extended replacement cost) as overlooked optional add-ons that fill standard policy gaps, framed as a 'you were never asked' awareness tip rather than a coverage limits or annual review angle.
scoring_notes: Both the East Cobb (78% homeowners) and Lewisville Lake (65% homeowners) audiences skew significantly toward homeownership; Perimeter is lower at 55% but still meaningful. Endorsements haven't been covered in the prior 6 months of tips — prior homeowners tips focused on coverage limits, annual review triggers, renovation underinsurance, and dwelling vs. personal property mechanics. This is a fresh category angle: optional add-ons vs. base coverage education. Evergreen-ish but actionable. Source is Consumer Reports, a trusted domain.

tip_title: Your Home Policy Has a Flood Blind Spot. Here's the One Thing That Fixes It.
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: Your Home Policy Has a Flood Blind Spot. Here's the One Thing That Fixes It.**

Standard homeowners and renters policies don't cover flood damage — full stop. That's not a technicality buried in the fine print; it's a fundamental gap that catches people off guard when heavy rain rolls through or a nearby waterway jumps its banks. The fix is a separate flood policy, available through FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program or through private insurers. The catch most people don't know: there's typically a 30-day waiting period before a new flood policy takes effect, which means you can't buy it the week a storm is threatening and expect coverage.

With August sitting squarely in peak storm season, it's worth checking whether you have a separate flood policy in place — and if not, talking to your Peachy agent now rather than when the radar starts lighting up.

📖 [Learn more from NAIC](https://content.naic.org/consumer/flood-insurance.htm)
summary: Covers the 30-day waiting period on new flood insurance policies as the reason to act before storm season peaks, framed as an urgency-of-timing angle rather than a basic 'flood isn't covered' education tip or an NFIP-vs-private comparison.
scoring_notes: August is peak Atlantic hurricane season and also peak North Texas storm season — high timeliness for all three newsletters. Both the Georgia and Lewisville Lake audiences have meaningful homeowner populations (78%, 55%, 65%). The 30-day waiting period angle is substantively different from prior flood tips: prior coverage on 06-14 explained flood isn't covered and NFIP exists; prior 07-20 tip compared NFIP vs. private options. This tip's angle is specifically the waiting-period clock as the reason to act *right now* in August — an urgency framing none of the prior tips used. Source is NAIC, a trusted domain.
